definition: Audio visual speech recognition (AVSR) is a technique that uses image processing capabilities in lip reading to aid speech recognition systems in recognizing indeterministic phones or giving preponderance among near probability decisions.
details: Each system of lip reading and speech recognition works separately, then their results are mixed at the stage of feature fusion. As the name suggests, it has two parts. First one is the audio part and second one is the visual part. In audio part we use features like log mel spectrogram, mfcc etc. from the raw audio samples and we build a model to get feature vector out of it . For visual part generally we use some variant of convolutional neural network to compress the image to a feature vector after that we concatenate these two vectors (audio and visual ) and try to predict the target object.

explainer.lead: Audio-visual speech recognition combines what a system hears with what it sees in a speaker’s lip movements. The extra visual evidence can help when the audio alone leaves several similarly likely interpretations.

tiers.eli5: It is like listening to a friend while also watching their mouth. If you cannot quite hear a sound, the shape of their lips can give you another clue. A computer can combine both clues to work out what was said.
tiers.practitioner: Build separate audio and visual feature extractors, such as log-mel spectrograms or MFCCs for audio and a convolutional neural network for images. Concatenate the resulting feature vectors and train a predictor on the fused representation. The audio and visual inputs must represent the same speech segment for this fusion to be useful.
tiers.paperLevel: AVSR combines audio-derived features with image-derived lip-reading features to improve recognition when acoustic evidence is uncertain. A typical formulation is a = A(x_audio), v = V(x_visual), z = [a; v], and y_hat = P(z), where A and V are separate feature extractors, concatenation performs feature fusion, and P predicts the target.

explainer.example: Suppose the audio model assigns nearly equal probability to two possible phones. The visual model processes the matching lip movements, and its feature vector is concatenated with the audio vector; the fused predictor can then favor the phone better supported by the combined evidence.

usedIn.name: Speech recognition with uncertain audio
usedIn.detail: Lip-reading evidence can help distinguish sounds or choose among nearly equally likely recognition decisions.

usedIn.name: Visual lip reading
usedIn.detail: Image processing supplies a complementary speech signal that can be fused with an acoustic recognizer.

explainer.intuition: Speech leaves clues in both sound and lip movement, so combining them can resolve ambiguity that remains in either signal alone. The key design choice is to extract each modality’s features separately before merging them.
howItWorks: Convert raw audio into features such as a log-mel spectrogram or MFCCs.
Pass the audio features through a model to obtain an audio feature vector.
Use a convolutional neural network variant to compress the visual input into a visual feature vector.
Concatenate the audio and visual vectors at the feature-fusion stage.
Use the fused vector to predict the recognition target.
explainer.whyItMatters: The visual stream provides additional evidence for recognizing indeterministic phones and breaking near-ties in acoustic decisions. Feature fusion lets one predictor use both representations rather than treating lip reading and speech recognition as unrelated tasks.
misconceptions: It is not lip reading alone: the audio and visual branches both contribute to the final prediction.
The branches are not necessarily fused as raw signals; the described approach concatenates their extracted feature vectors.
A visual feature vector does not replace acoustic features; it supplements them.

diagram.caption: Separate audio and visual encoders produce feature vectors, which are concatenated for the final prediction.
